question: What is the primary biological purpose of the inflammatory response?

options.A: To contain injurious agents and initiate tissue repair
options.B: To increase the circulating red blood cell mass
options.C: To permanently lower the core body temperature
options.D: To permanently replace damaged tissue with scar tissue

explanation: Inflammation acts as a defense mechanism to neutralize threats and clear cellular debris before healing can begin. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why can an overactive inflammatory response be harmful to the body?

options.A: It prevents any form of blood clotting from occurring
options.B: It damages healthy host tissues alongside the invading agents
options.C: It immediately destroys the bone marrow and stops immunity
options.D: It permanently halts all cellular division in the body

explanation: While protective, the powerful chemicals released during inflammation can inflict collateral damage on healthy surrounding cells. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which cell type is the primary cellular hallmark of acute inflammation?
explanation: Neutrophils are the first responders, arriving rapidly in large numbers during the acute phase of tissue injury. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h2)

question: A key pathological feature that distinguishes chronic inflammation from acute inflammation is the presence of...
explanation: Chronic inflammation involves long-term immune activity featuring macrophages, lymphocytes, tissue destruction, and scarring. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the physiological cause of the swelling (tumor) seen in acute inflammation?

options.A: Deposition of excessive calcium crystals in the tissue
options.B: Complete cessation of lymphatic drainage in the limb
options.C: Rapid proliferation of local skeletal muscle fibers
options.D: Accumulation of fluid and exudate in the interstitial space

explanation: Increased vascular permeability allows protein-rich fluid to leak out of blood vessels into the tissues, causing localized swelling. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which chemical mediators are primarily responsible for the sensation of pain during an inflammatory response?
explanation: These inflammatory mediators directly sensitize local nociceptors and nerve endings, transmitting pain signals to the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the sequence of leukocyte emigration during the cellular response?
explanation: White blood cells first drift to the vessel margins, roll along the lining, stick firmly, slip through the gap, and follow chemical trails to the injury site. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why does vascular permeability increase during acute inflammation?

options.A: To allow plasma proteins and leukocytes to enter the injured tissue
options.B: To prevent red blood cells from escaping into the lymphatic system
options.C: To flush out excess carbon dioxide from the local interstitial space
options.D: To maintain a constant blood pressure within the microvasculature

explanation: Increased permeability creates gaps in the vessel walls, permitting essential immune cells and proteins to reach the site of injury or infection. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h4)

question: What does a 'shift to the left' in a differential white blood cell count typically indicate?

options.A: An increase in immature neutrophils responding to acute infection
options.B: A chronic viral infection with depressed lymphocyte counts
options.C: A severe deficiency of circulating platelets and clotting factors
options.D: An allergic reaction mediated primarily by resting basophils

explanation: When the bone marrow rapidly releases white blood cells to combat acute demand, many immature forms (bands) appear in the peripheral blood. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which laboratory marker rises most rapidly in the blood following the onset of acute tissue inflammation?
explanation: CRP is synthesized by the liver and acts as a sensitive, rapid-response indicator of active systemic inflammation. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h5)

question: A patient with a deep surgical wound develops a fever, tachycardia, and increasing wound pain. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Discharge the patient with instructions to rest at home
options.B: Assess the wound for signs of infection and notify the physician
options.C: Restrict all oral fluid intake to prevent systemic edema
options.D: Administer a warm compress and document normal healing

explanation: Systemic signs combined with worsening local pain point toward a developing wound infection that requires prompt medical evaluation. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which type of wound exudate is thick, opaque, and typically indicates the presence of white blood cells and bacterial breakdown?
explanation: Purulent drainage (pus) consists of dead neutrophils, tissue debris, and microorganisms commonly found in infected wounds. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h6)

question: How do Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) primarily reduce inflammation?

options.A: By causing widespread vasoconstriction of major arteries
options.B: By stimulating the bone marrow to produce mature lymphocytes
options.C: By inhibiting cyclooxygenase and blocking prostaglandin production
options.D: By directly destroying invading bacterial cell walls in the blood

explanation: NSAIDs block the COX enzymes responsible for synthesizing prostaglandins, which mediate pain and inflammation. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h7)

question: A patient is prescribed high-dose systemic corticosteroids for a severe inflammatory condition. Which assessment finding requires the most immediate vigilance by the nurse?

options.A: Severe localized vasoconstriction in the peripheral digits
options.B: A sudden drop in the patient's body temperature below 35°C
options.C: An increase in total red blood cell count and hemoglobin
options.D: Signs of a new infection or elevated blood glucose

explanation: Corticosteroids suppress the immune system, masking infection signs and raising blood sugar levels, requiring careful monitoring. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is a major risk of stopping prescribed anti-inflammatory or antibiotic therapy prematurely when symptoms improve?

options.A: Complete cessation of all white blood cell production
options.B: Permanent systemic immunity to all future pathogen exposures
options.C: Instantaneous development of chronic kidney failure
options.D: Rebound inflammation or resurgence of the underlying infection

explanation: Halting medication before the inflammatory trigger or pathogen is fully eradicated often leads to a recurrence of symptoms. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical complication of prolonged, uncontrolled chronic inflammation?

options.B: Complete and permanent regeneration of normal, unscarred parenchymal tissue
options.C: Extensive fibrosis and scar tissue formation

explanation: Chronic inflammation typically leads to tissue destruction and scarring (fibrosis) rather than perfect structural regeneration. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h8)
